bridges.mechanism: Higher rates of commercial vessel transits relieve port backlogs and keep scheduled deliveries on time, whereas reductions in transit throughput directly produce rerouting, delays and inventory shortfalls that raise measured supply-chain disruption.

Sharp increases in war‑risk insurance premiums act as a real‑time signal of acute geopolitical stress and higher trade costs, prompting rapid portfolio rebalancing and margin dynamics that raise short‑term and intraday volatility in bond yields.

Higher war‑risk insurance premiums for shipments transiting the region raise expected project costs and delivery risk for capital‑intensive AI infrastructure, causing investors and operators to delay or reduce new commitments.

Significant redeployment of US/Allied naval and ISR assets to protect regional shipping in the Iran–US flashpoints reduces available deterrent and intelligence support in Europe, lowering the cost of escalation for Russia and enabling higher kinetic tempo in Ukraine.

An intensification of maritime security operations that secures chokepoints and escorts commercial shipments shortens delivery delays for racks, chips and other hardware, enabling faster on‑premises and cloud compute deployments.

A sustained increase in oil export flows lowers global crude prices and near‑term headline inflation, causing market participants to scale back the probability and magnitude of anticipated central‑bank rate hikes.

A sustained drop in regional oil export flows drives fuel, logistics and energy‑price spikes that force fabs to curtail runs or postpone capacity expansions because of higher operating costs and disrupted inputs.

A rise in the assessed probability of energy‑supply disruptions raises expected future inflation and adds a term‑risk premium, directly pushing up long‑maturity bond yields as investors demand compensation for higher expected price and tail risks.

An elevated assessed risk of Middle East supply disruptions causes immediate global price shocks and reallocation of LNG/oil cargoes away from Europe, directly increasing the magnitude and likelihood of energy shortfalls tied to the Russia–Ukraine war.

A rising assessed risk of energy and transit disruption from an Iran–US confrontation prompts the US and allied governments to adopt export controls, investment screening and supply‑chain security measures that directly harden technology trade frictions with China.

Rising perceived risk of energy or commodity interruptions leads governments to impose export controls, emergency tariffs or quotas and other protective measures to conserve domestic supplies, increasing effective trade barriers.

Higher expected probability and severity of supply disruptions raises uncertainty about commodity prices and corporate earnings, prompting greater price swings across equity, credit and commodity markets.

Conflict escalation drives flight‑to‑quality into long‑duration government bonds while short‑term policy rates stay unchanged, compressing long minus short yields and flattening (or inverting) the curve.

A marked escalation in kinetic activity and high-profile strikes in the Russia–Ukraine theater amplifies global war-risk perceptions, prompting insurers to raise war-risk and political-risk premiums on shipments transiting exposed Middle Eastern chokepoints.

A marked uptick in kinetic operations raises policymakers' threat perceptions and domestic political pressure, prompting faster adoption of technology export controls, investment screening and adversarial rhetoric that heighten tech-sector geopolitical tensions.
Escalation in kinetic operations raises geopolitical risk premia and triggers rapid re‑pricing across commodity, equity and credit markets, directly increasing short‑term asset price volatility.
Large disruptions to oil and gas flows lift headline inflation and forward inflation swaps, prompting markets to price in earlier and/or larger central‑bank tightening.

Sharp disruptions to Russian energy supplies push importers (particularly in Europe and Asia) to replace lost barrels with increased purchases from Middle Eastern producers, raising crude and product export volumes transiting regional sea lanes.

Acute energy supply disruptions and higher electricity prices force cloud providers and hyperscalers to delay or scale back data-center builds and machine deployments in affected regions, directly slowing the rate at which new AI compute capacity is brought online.

Severe energy disruptions raise domestic production costs and political pressure to shield energy‑intensive industries, prompting policymakers to adopt higher tariffs, import restrictions or selective export controls to protect domestic capacity.

More stringent sanctions and export-control measures tied to the conflict lead suppliers and governments to restrict sales of advanced lithography tools, materials and design software to targeted jurisdictions, delaying fab tool deliveries and new wafer-line ramps and therefore reducing near-term semiconductor manufacturing capacity growth.

Expanded and tightened sanctions and export controls targeting Russia and counterparties directly restrict exports of critical inputs (e.g., neon, palladium, dual‑use components) and payment/transport channels, causing immediate procurement delays and shortages in U.S. supply chains.

Frequent expansions and legal complexity of sanctions and related trade controls create ambiguity about permitted trade flows and classifications, increasing unpredictability in U.S. tariff decisions and enforcement for affected firms.

Sustained large military aid packages raise fiscal and geopolitical uncertainty for donor and regional economies, triggering frequent portfolio rebalancing and spikes in sovereign yield and swap volatility.

Large, sustained flows of Western military aid and associated escort/escrow logistics to Ukraine require redeployment and retention of naval and air assets in the Atlantic/European theatre, reducing available US/ally maritime forces and patrols allocated to protect Middle Eastern sea lanes.
Faster on‑ramps of AI compute capacity require immediate procurement of GPUs, accelerators and supporting semiconductors, directly increasing near‑term component demand.

Large, rapid inbound capital directed to AI infrastructure tightens domestic financial conditions and boosts asset prices, causing markets to revise up expected future policy rates to counter overheating.

A meaningful shortfall in semiconductor manufacturing capacity raises expectations of persistent supply constraints and sectoral price pressure, increasing inflation risk premia embedded in long-term bond yields.

A sustained increase (or decrease) in advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity—especially in major Asian economies—changes industrial and data‑centre activity and therefore short‑to‑medium‑term oil demand, which translates into higher (or lower) volumes of crude and refined exports transiting Middle East sea lanes within months.

Incremental increases in domestic or allied semiconductor manufacturing capacity relieve foundry bottlenecks and inventory shortages, directly reducing the frequency and severity of supply‑chain disruptions for chip‑dependent goods.

Escalating tech geopolitics (sanctions, export controls, sudden corporate delistings) forces rapid sectoral repricing and risk-reassessment by fixed-income investors, producing abrupt swings in credit spreads and government bond yields.

A spike in tech-geopolitical tension prompts the US and regional partners to expand naval patrols, convoy escorts and allied presence to deter retaliation or interdiction tied to technology disputes, directly raising aggregate maritime security commitments.

Heightened tech rivalry increases the incidence and perceived risk of state or proxy cyber/kinetic attacks on maritime logistics and insurers' exposure, leading underwriters to raise war‑risk and political‑risk premiums for Gulf transits.

Rising tech tensions increase incentives for state and proxy actors to use maritime harassment, strikes on shipping or infrastructure, and asymmetric measures as leverage, directly raising the probability and expected severity of energy‑supply disruptions from the region.

Rising tech geopolitical tension prompts governments to expand export controls and coordinated sanction lists that explicitly target dual‑use AI/semiconductor suppliers and financial facilitators connected to Russia, increasing overall sanctions stringency.

Spikes in tech geopolitical tension prompt ad hoc export controls, sanctions and tariff threat statements from policymakers and regulators, directly increasing unpredictability about upcoming tariff decisions and enforcement.
Rising geopolitical competition over AI/tech leads governments to enact concrete measures—tariffs, formal export controls, investment screens and quotas—raising the effective level of trade barriers.

Rising expectations of higher policy rates increase insurers' and reinsurers' cost-of-capital and prompt tighter risk-tolerance and repricing of tail exposures, leading underwriters to raise war‑risk and political‑risk premiums on shipments through the Gulf.

Rising expectations of higher policy rates increase government borrowing costs and crowd fiscal space, making legislatures and treasuries less willing or able to approve new or larger external military aid packages.

Rising expected policy rates directly raise investors' discount rates and borrowing costs, reducing venture and project finance availability and thus lowering net capital flows into AI infrastructure.

Rising expected policy rates tighten trade finance and raise rollover costs for suppliers and logistics firms, increasing bankruptcies, credit distress and inventory shortages that produce supply‑chain disruptions.

A loss of central bank credibility raises perceived macro and currency risk for investors, prompting reallocation or withdrawal of long‑term investments away from capital‑intensive AI infrastructure projects.

Higher central-bank credibility lowers political pressure to deploy ad‑hoc trade measures to stabilise growth or markets, reducing the frequency and unpredictability of tariff announcements (and the reverse when credibility falls).

A sustained rise in long‑term yields raises global borrowing costs and dampens investment and industrial demand, reducing crude demand and thereby lowering oil export volumes transiting Middle East chokepoints.

Higher long-term yields raise financing and rollover costs for commodity traders, shipping firms and energy infrastructure projects, prompting reductions in shipments, inventories and investment in alternate routes that increase the likelihood and severity of energy supply disruptions.

Higher long‑term yields increase the cost of financing multi‑year, capital‑intensive fab builds and depress project NPVs, causing firms to delay, scale back, or cancel semiconductor capacity expansions.

Rising long-term yields raise corporate and consumer financing costs and lift discount rates, which dampens capex and demand for durable goods and thereby reduces semiconductor orders over the product-cycle.

Sharp increases in bond yield volatility signal elevated systemic risk and funding stress, provoking immediate risk‑off behavior among underwriters and reinsurers and materially raising war‑risk and political‑risk insurance premia for regional shipping.

Spikes in bond-yield volatility disrupt trade finance, export credit and insurance markets that underwrite arms production and shipments, delaying deliveries and lowering the operational tempo and overall intensity of military operations.

Spikes in bond yield volatility amplify market stress and policymakers' risk aversion, provoking defensive regulatory responses (heightened screening of cross‑border tech deals, controls or capital restrictions) that increase tech geopolitical tension.

Spikes in bond-yield volatility force frequent revaluation of discount rates and risk premia, provoking rapid repricing in equities and credit and thus directly increasing short‑term asset-price volatility.

Spikes in asset‑price volatility raise financial‑stability concerns and prompt markets to price earlier or larger central‑bank easing (or a pause in tightening), reducing expected future policy rates.

Elevated short-term volatility raises cost of capital and reduces risk appetite among institutional and venture investors, leading to reduced fundraising and slower deployment of financing for large-scale AI data centers and accelerator purchases.

An increase in domestic semiconductor demand diverts scarce chips and related components toward civilian supply chains and domestic programs, constraining availability for platforms and munitions destined for Ukraine and thereby reducing aid flow rates.
Sustained supply‑chain disruptions reduce expected long‑run GDP growth and capital demand, lowering the growth component of long‑term yields and putting downward pressure on those yields.

Escalating supply-chain disruptions tied to US protectionist measures push US firms and policymakers to prioritize secure maritime corridors, prompting increased naval escorts, patrols and allied security deployments in the Middle East to protect vulnerable shipments.

Heightened supply‑chain disruptions increase delays and component shortages for weapons and ammunition production, directly reducing the rate and timeliness of external military aid deliveries to Ukraine.

Visible supply interruptions for critical tech components prompt governments to announce defensive industrial measures and export controls and to publicly assign blame, escalating bilateral tech policy friction and geopolitical tension.

Greater uncertainty about future tariff policies increases rapid, discrete revisions to inflation and corporate-profit forecasts, driving more frequent repricing in the bond market and higher yield volatility.

Rising unpredictability in US tariff policy increases underwriters' perceived political and operational risk for international routes, causing war‑risk and political‑risk insurers to raise premiums for shipments transiting volatile Middle East sea lanes.

Rising unpredictability about tariff and trade enforcement increases jurisdictional policy risk and investor uncertainty, prompting funds and corporate investors to pause or re-allocate commitments to multi-year AI infrastructure projects.
Higher trade barriers push up import costs and near‑term inflation expectations and raise term premia as investors price policy uncertainty and protectionism risks, lifting long‑term bond yields.

Higher US trade barriers quickly reduce bilateral and intermediate goods trade volumes, directly lowering container and bulk ship voyages that transit Middle East chokepoints (Suez/Strait of Hormuz) as shippers curtail shipments and demand for route capacity falls.

Rising tariffs, quotas or other trade barriers raise costs and administrative frictions for cross‑border procurement of weapons and dual‑use components, slowing or lowering the volume of military aid transferred to Ukraine.

Higher trade barriers and export controls directly block or raise the cost of importing critical fab equipment, precursor chemicals and specialized machinery, forcing delays or cancellations of planned semiconductor fab expansions and reducing near-term installed capacity.

nodes.label: Spare oil production capacity

nodes.label: Strategic petroleum reserve level
nodes.description: The quantity of government-held emergency petroleum stocks available for release to stabilize supply.

nodes.label: Market volatility expectation
nodes.description: The market-implied expectation of near-term price volatility for oil and energy markets.

nodes.label: Degree of commercial normalization
nodes.description: The extent to which commercial actors (shippers, insurers, traders) resume pre-crisis operational patterns and risk tolerances.

nodes.label: Non-state maritime militia activity
nodes.description: The intensity and operational tempo of non-state armed groups conducting attacks or interdictions affecting maritime traffic.

nodes.label: Alternative route and transit capacity
nodes.description: The available throughput capacity of alternate shipping routes, pipelines, and terminals to absorb rerouted flows.

nodes.label: Energy supply disruption risk

nodes.label: Rate of transnational infrastructure attacks
nodes.description: Measures the frequency per unit time of cross-border strikes and sabotage against energy, transport and logistics infrastructure.

nodes.label: Severity of energy supply disruptions
nodes.description: Measures the magnitude of interruptions to the availability and delivery of energy commodities and refined products.

nodes.label: Stringency of sanctions measures
nodes.description: Measures the overall restrictiveness and comprehensiveness of economic, trade and financial sanctions regimes in effect.

nodes.label: Rate of sanctions exemptions/carve-outs
nodes.description: Measures the flow rate at which exemptions, carve-outs or waivers to sanctions are granted, amended or rescinded.

nodes.label: Legislative and regulatory sanction momentum
nodes.description: Measures the pace and directional momentum of policymaking activity (bills, votes, regulatory changes) that alters sanctions regimes.

nodes.label: Degree of diplomatic alignment
nodes.description: Measures the extent to which principal actors present coordinated diplomatic positions and policy convergence on the crises.

nodes.label: Rate of external military aid flows
nodes.description: Measures the flow rate of material, financing and capability transfers to parties engaged in the conflicts.

nodes.label: Cohesion among allied actors
nodes.description: Measures the stability and cooperative coherence of security and political alignments among allied groups over time.

nodes.label: Global energy price level
nodes.description: Measures prevailing market prices for key energy commodities and refined fuels on global markets.

nodes.label: Market risk premium for affected sectors
nodes.description: Measures the additional cost of capital or price markup demanded by markets for exposure to sectors impacted by the crises.

nodes.label: Logistics and transport network throughput
nodes.description: Measures the volumetric flow of goods and freight moving through critical transport nodes and corridors per unit time.

nodes.label: Level of industrial input scarcity
nodes.description: Measures the accumulated shortfall in availability of critical industrial components, fuels or feedstocks that constrain production.

nodes.label: Strategic escalation pressure
nodes.description: Measures the latent propensity and systemic pressure toward wider or intensified escalation between actors or theatres.

nodes.label: Public and political support for foreign engagement
nodes.description: Measures the level of domestic public and political backing for continued or increased external military, financial or diplomatic engagement.

nodes.label: Degree of financial transaction restrictions
nodes.description: Measures the extent to which cross-border payments, banking links and financial services are constrained by controls, de-risking or sanctions.

nodes.label: AI compute deployment rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate at which new AI compute capacity is brought online per unit time.

nodes.label: Capital flows to AI infrastructure
nodes.description: Measures net financial investment and financing volumes directed to AI infrastructure projects and related assets per period.

nodes.label: Concentration of financing
nodes.description: Measures the extent to which financing for AI infrastructure is concentrated among a small number of financiers or funding channels.

nodes.label: Project leverage ratio
nodes.description: Measures average debt-to-equity (or debt-to-assets) leverage used across AI infrastructure projects.

nodes.label: Credit market tightness
nodes.description: Measures perceived cost and availability of credit for infrastructure and corporate borrowers in credit markets.

nodes.label: Asset valuation gap
nodes.description: Measures the divergence between market valuations of AI-related assets and their estimated fundamental cash flows or underlying economic productivity.

nodes.label: Supply-chain resilience
nodes.description: Measures the ability of component and equipment supply chains to deliver required inputs for AI infrastructure without delay or disruption.

nodes.label: Semiconductor manufacturing capacity
nodes.description: Measures installed throughput and capability for producing advanced semiconductor wafers, tools, and related components needed for AI hardware.

nodes.label: Tech geopolitical tension
nodes.description: Measures the intensity of geopolitical competition and policy measures that affect technology trade, investment and collaboration flows.

nodes.label: Regulatory intervention pressure
nodes.description: Measures the frequency, scope and severity of regulatory actions, restrictions or policy interventions targeting AI infrastructure, markets or finance.

nodes.label: Cybersecurity vulnerability level
nodes.description: Measures prevalence and severity of operational security weaknesses and the incidence rate of cyber breaches affecting AI systems and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment volatility
nodes.description: Measures variability and intensity of investor sentiment and confidence relating to AI infrastructure investments and related equities.

nodes.label: Energy supply stability and cost
nodes.description: Measures the reliability of electricity supply and the stability of unit energy costs available to power large-scale data centers.

nodes.label: Compute ownership concentration
nodes.description: Measures the share of total AI compute resources controlled by the largest operators relative to the rest of the market.

nodes.label: Compute efficiency improvement rate
nodes.description: Measures the rate of technological improvement in compute performance per unit cost and per watt over time.

Policy interest rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing short‑term policy interest rate set as the reference cost of borrowing in the monetary policy framework.

nodes.label: Policy rate expectations
nodes.description: Market and investor expectations about the future path of the policy interest rate over relevant horizons.

nodes.label: Monetary authority credibility
nodes.description: The perceived reliability of monetary authorities to achieve announced objectives such as inflation control and financial stability.

nodes.label: Policy communication clarity
nodes.description: The degree of clarity, consistency and predictability in public monetary and macrofinancial communications.

nodes.label: Short-term bond yield
nodes.description: The market yield prevailing on short‑maturity fixed‑income instruments reflecting near‑term interest rates.

nodes.label: Long-term bond yield
nodes.description: The market yield prevailing on long‑maturity fixed‑income instruments that reflects longer‑run rate expectations and risk premia.

nodes.label: Yield curve slope
nodes.description: The difference between long‑term and short‑term bond yields, indicating term structure steepness or inversion.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: The component of long‑term yields attributable to compensation for interest‑rate risk and uncertainty beyond expectations of policy rates.

nodes.label: Yield volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude and frequency of fluctuations in bond yields across maturities, capturing market turbulence in fixed income.

nodes.label: Market liquidity conditions
nodes.description: The ease and cost of executing trades in financial markets, measured by bid‑ask spreads, depth and immediacy.

nodes.label: Investor bond positioning
nodes.description: The aggregate stock of investors' net exposures to bonds and fixed‑income strategies across funds and accounts.

nodes.label: Hedging and leverage flow
nodes.description: The rate of derivative and financing activity used for hedging or leveraged speculative positions that changes exposures over time.

nodes.label: Cross‑border capital flows
nodes.description: The net flow of capital across jurisdictions into and out of domestic financial assets and liabilities per unit time.

nodes.label: Credit spread level
nodes.description: The average premium demanded over risk‑free yields to compensate investors for credit and default risk in non‑sovereign debt.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Market and survey‑based anticipations of future inflation rates over short and medium horizons.

nodes.label: Real economic growth rate
nodes.description: The continuous rate of change in real economic output, reflecting underlying demand and supply dynamics.

Investor sentiment
nodes.description: The aggregate market mood reflecting risk appetite and collective willingness to buy or sell risky assets.

nodes.label: Asset price volatility
nodes.description: The degree of short-term variability in asset prices across equity and credit markets.

nodes.label: Trading volume flow
nodes.description: The rate and net magnitude of executed trades and turnover moving through financial markets over time.

nodes.label: Capital allocation to technology
nodes.description: The stock share or level of investable capital directed toward technology-related sectors and instruments.

nodes.label: Semiconductor demand
nodes.description: The aggregate level of end-market demand for semiconductor products and related components.

nodes.label: Automobile sales demand
nodes.description: The overall consumer and fleet demand for passenger and commercial vehicles in relevant markets.

nodes.label: Corporate earnings expectations
nodes.description: The consensus forecasted profit levels for corporates as priced by analysts and markets.

nodes.label: Guidance revision rate
nodes.description: The frequency and magnitude at which firms change forward guidance and earnings outlooks.

nodes.label: Employment change rate
nodes.description: The net rate of hiring and layoffs occurring across firms in the affected sectors.

nodes.label: Supply chain disruption level
nodes.description: The extent to which production and logistic pathways are impaired, delayed, or capacity-constrained.

nodes.label: Tariff policy uncertainty
nodes.description: The degree of unpredictability and ambiguity surrounding trade barrier decisions and enforcement.

nodes.label: Trade barrier level
nodes.description: The effective intensity of tariffs, quotas, and trade costs affecting cross-border goods and services.

nodes.label: Monetary policy tightness
nodes.description: The prevailing stance of monetary policy measured by real interest rates and liquidity conditions set by policy authorities.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market and public expectation for future inflation rates over relevant horizons.

nodes.label: Corporate cost-cutting rate
nodes.description: The pace at which firms implement expense-reduction actions such as restructurings, layoffs, and spending cuts.

nodes.label: Market liquidity level
nodes.description: The ease with which assets can be bought or sold without large price concessions across equity and credit markets.

Higher long‑term yields increase the cost of financing multi‑year, capital‑intensive fab builds and depress project NPVs, causing firms to delay, scale back, or cancel semiconductor capacity expansions.

Rising long-term yields raise corporate and consumer financing costs and lift discount rates, which dampens capex and demand for durable goods and thereby reduces semiconductor orders over the product-cycle.

Sharp increases in bond yield volatility signal elevated systemic risk and funding stress, provoking immediate risk‑off behavior among underwriters and reinsurers and materially raising war‑risk and political‑risk insurance premia for regional shipping.

Spikes in bond-yield volatility disrupt trade finance, export credit and insurance markets that underwrite arms production and shipments, delaying deliveries and lowering the operational tempo and overall intensity of military operations.

Spikes in bond yield volatility amplify market stress and policymakers' risk aversion, provoking defensive regulatory responses (heightened screening of cross‑border tech deals, controls or capital restrictions) that increase tech geopolitical tension.

Spikes in bond-yield volatility force frequent revaluation of discount rates and risk premia, provoking rapid repricing in equities and credit and thus directly increasing short‑term asset-price volatility.

Spikes in asset‑price volatility raise financial‑stability concerns and prompt markets to price earlier or larger central‑bank easing (or a pause in tightening), reducing expected future policy rates.

Elevated short-term volatility raises cost of capital and reduces risk appetite among institutional and venture investors, leading to reduced fundraising and slower deployment of financing for large-scale AI data centers and accelerator purchases.

An increase in domestic semiconductor demand diverts scarce chips and related components toward civilian supply chains and domestic programs, constraining availability for platforms and munitions destined for Ukraine and thereby reducing aid flow rates.
Sustained supply‑chain disruptions reduce expected long‑run GDP growth and capital demand, lowering the growth component of long‑term yields and putting downward pressure on those yields.

Escalating supply-chain disruptions tied to US protectionist measures push US firms and policymakers to prioritize secure maritime corridors, prompting increased naval escorts, patrols and allied security deployments in the Middle East to protect vulnerable shipments.

Heightened supply‑chain disruptions increase delays and component shortages for weapons and ammunition production, directly reducing the rate and timeliness of external military aid deliveries to Ukraine.

Visible supply interruptions for critical tech components prompt governments to announce defensive industrial measures and export controls and to publicly assign blame, escalating bilateral tech policy friction and geopolitical tension.

Greater uncertainty about future tariff policies increases rapid, discrete revisions to inflation and corporate-profit forecasts, driving more frequent repricing in the bond market and higher yield volatility.

Rising unpredictability in US tariff policy increases underwriters' perceived political and operational risk for international routes, causing war‑risk and political‑risk insurers to raise premiums for shipments transiting volatile Middle East sea lanes.

Rising unpredictability about tariff and trade enforcement increases jurisdictional policy risk and investor uncertainty, prompting funds and corporate investors to pause or re-allocate commitments to multi-year AI infrastructure projects.
Higher trade barriers push up import costs and near‑term inflation expectations and raise term premia as investors price policy uncertainty and protectionism risks, lifting long‑term bond yields.

Higher US trade barriers quickly reduce bilateral and intermediate goods trade volumes, directly lowering container and bulk ship voyages that transit Middle East chokepoints (Suez/Strait of Hormuz) as shippers curtail shipments and demand for route capacity falls.

Rising tariffs, quotas or other trade barriers raise costs and administrative frictions for cross‑border procurement of weapons and dual‑use components, slowing or lowering the volume of military aid transferred to Ukraine.

Higher trade barriers and export controls directly block or raise the cost of importing critical fab equipment, precursor chemicals and specialized machinery, forcing delays or cancellations of planned semiconductor fab expansions and reducing near-term installed capacity.
